evidenceAudit.scope: Adult after the death of a family member or close person, seen in a Saudi primary health centre, hospital ward or emergency department: supporting normal grief, culturally and religiously informed communication, identifying people at risk of prolonged grief disorder, screening and referral, and when to treat comorbid depression, post-traumatic stress or suicide risk. Draws on the ICD-11 definition, Arabic-speaking and Saudi cohorts and treatment reviews. Not for children and adolescents, perinatal loss, or detailed psychotherapy delivery.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-20.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi Ministry of Health or Saudi mental health guideline for bereavement care was found; NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries bereavement content is restricted to the United Kingdom and could not be read. The pathway is built from the ICD-11 definition papers and research studies, so it is expert synthesis rather than a national guideline.

Saudi data are limited to one study of 226 undergraduate students (12% met prolonged grief criteria), quoted second-hand from the Arabic-speaking cohort paper; the original paper was not read. The main Arabic-speaking cohort is online and treatment-seeking (1,051 people, 19.3% from Saudi Arabia, 73.5% women, mean age 25) and does not represent the Saudi population.

The Islamic mourning guidance is a single newspaper religious-advice column (three days for relatives, four months and ten days for a widow). It is not a scholarly fatwa; confirm with the family and with hospital chaplaincy or religious affairs before applying it.

No medicine is written. The pharmacotherapy review found only open-label SSRI trials and one randomised nortriptyline trial in bereavement-related depression; none showed a proven grief-specific drug benefit. Treat comorbid depression by the depression topic.

Brief screening tools for prolonged grief (Prolonged Grief-13, Inventory of Complicated Grief-Revised, International Prolonged Grief Disorder Scale) are cited from research papers; a validated Saudi Arabic version was not verified. Cut-offs (PG-13 score of 32 or more in the Saudi student study) are research thresholds, not diagnostic.

One review argues that the evidence separating prolonged grief disorder from normal grief and its societal effects are still contested (PMC10291380, abstract only was read); use clinical judgement and avoid pathologising normal grief.

The Rosner treatment manual and effect sizes (Shear's complicated grief treatment pre-post effect size 1.63) come from a 2011 German article; generalisability to Saudi Arabia is unknown and no Saudi-adapted therapy was found.

Suicide risk assessment, post-traumatic stress disorder and depression treatment are only referred to; refer to the corresponding topics. Specialist content for children, perinatal loss and loss by suicide or homicide needs separate guidance.
Figures were read by automated extraction of the articles; spot-check each number against the source during clinical review.
Blood tests (full blood count, thyroid function, glucose) are included as clinical judgement for people with somatic symptoms; the cited guideline does not name them.
NICE NG222 is a depression guideline used here for the depression and suicide assessment steps; it is not bereavement-specific.
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so no medicine registration was checked.

pathophysiology.summary: Grief after the death of a loved one is a normal yet painful process; it varies with culture, gender, personality and circumstances, and for most people symptoms fall substantially by 6 months (Treatment of complicated grief, Section Introduction). A small group develop prolonged grief disorder: persistent longing for or preoccupation with the deceased with intense emotional pain and functional impairment lasting more than 6 months and exceeding expected social, cultural or religious norms (ICD-11 prolonged grief disorder review, Section Table 1). Prolonged grief disorder is distinct from depression and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) though often comorbid with them (Treatment of complicated grief, Section Abstract). About 10% of bereaved people develop prolonged grief disorder after a natural loss, and nearly 50% after sudden or violent losses such as accidents, suicide, homicide or war (Arabic-speaking cohort, Section Introduction).

symptoms: Yearning or constant preoccupation with the deceased (ICD-11 prolonged grief disorder review, Section Table 1).
Intense emotional pain such as sadness, guilt, anger, denial or blame; emotional numbness; feeling that part of oneself has died (ICD-11 prolonged grief disorder review, Section Table 1).
Difficulty accepting the death or engaging in social or other activities (ICD-11 prolonged grief disorder review, Section Table 1).
Disturbed sleep, crying and sadness, which overlap with depression (Pharmacotherapy review, Section Introduction).
physicalSigns: Observed functional decline in personal, family, social, educational or occupational roles (ICD-11 prolonged grief disorder review, Section Table 1).
Social withdrawal or low perceived support (Arabic-speaking cohort, Section Results).
redFlags: Suicidal thoughts, plans or acts: assess immediately and arrange urgent mental health review (Pharmacotherapy review, Section Introduction notes suicidal ideation can occur in grief and depression).
Psychotic symptoms, severe self-neglect or inability to care for dependants: urgent psychiatric assessment (Pharmacotherapy review, Section Introduction).
Sudden or violent loss, loss of a child, or multiple losses: higher risk of prolonged grief, so offer early follow-up (Arabic-speaking cohort, Section Introduction).
Benzodiazepines are not advised for grief: in a trial they did not reduce grief and worsened sleep, and long-term dependence was reported (Pharmacotherapy review, Section Benzodiazepines).
precipitants: Female gender (odds ratio 1.75 for women compared with men) (Arabic-speaking cohort, Section Results).
Loss of a close family member, mostly a parent in that cohort (odds ratio 2.83) (Arabic-speaking cohort, Section Results).
A higher number of losses and traumatic events (Arabic-speaking cohort, Section Results).
Severe functional impairment in the first year (odds ratio 2.07) and low perceived social support (Arabic-speaking cohort, Section Results).
Sudden or violent death, such as accident, suicide or homicide (Arabic-speaking cohort, Section Introduction).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Painful but decreasing over the first months, with functioning preserved or recovering; longer grief that is within the person's cultural and religious norms is not a disorder (ICD-11 prolonged grief disorder review, Section Table 1).
Persistent longing or preoccupation, emotional pain and impairment for more than 6 months, exceeding cultural norms (ICD-11 prolonged grief disorder review, Section Table 1).
Pervasive low mood and loss of interest not tied only to the deceased; may coexist with grief (Pharmacotherapy review, Section Introduction).
Fear-based reaction to a threatening event with intrusion and avoidance, whereas grief is attachment-loss based (Pharmacotherapy review, Section Introduction).

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Daily yearning or emotional pain, 6 months or more since loss, at least five accompanying symptoms and functional impairment; score of 32 or more suggests risk in Saudi students
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Structured self-report that closely matches the ICD-11 criteria and has been used in Arabic-speaking samples (Arabic-speaking cohort, Section Materials and methods).
ruleIn.normalValue: Sum score below 32 and no daily separation distress

clinicalManagement.title: Offer immediate support and respect religious practice
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At the time of death and first days
actions: Communicate the death clearly and kindly; dissatisfaction with how the death was told is a risk factor (Arabic-speaking cohort, Section Introduction).

Facilitate religious and family rituals: in Saudi Arabia families receive condolences over about three days, and Islamic guidance limits outward mourning to three days except for a widow (Arab News mourning guidance, Section Hadith on mourning).
Help the family with practical needs, because condolence gatherings can be tiring and costly (Arab News mourning guidance, Section Solace customs).

clinicalManagement.title: Explain that grief is normal and usually settles
actions: Explain that sadness, crying, poor sleep and yearning are normal, and most people improve by 6 months (Treatment of complicated grief, Section Introduction).
Do not label normal grief as an illness; grief within cultural and religious norms is not a disorder (ICD-11 prolonged grief disorder review, Section Table 1).
Encourage family and community support, because low perceived support is linked to prolonged grief (Arabic-speaking cohort, Section Results).

clinicalManagement.title: Identify people at higher risk
actions: Flag sudden or violent death, loss of a child or parent, several losses, women, early severe impairment and low support (Arabic-speaking cohort, Section Results).
Offer a follow-up contact at about 1 and 3 months for these people (not stated in the sources; local practice).

clinicalManagement.title: Review at 6 months and screen
clinicalManagement.timeframe: 6 months or more after the loss
actions: Ask about persistent yearning, preoccupation and functioning; use the Prolonged Grief-13 where available (Arabic-speaking cohort, Section Materials and methods).
Consider cultural norms before diagnosing; longer grief within norms is not disorder (ICD-11 prolonged grief disorder review, Section Table 1).
Screen for depression, post-traumatic stress and suicide risk (NICE NG222 depression guideline, Recommendation 1.2.1 and 1.2.8).

clinicalManagement.title: Refer for grief-focused therapy
clinicalManagement.timeframe: When prolonged grief disorder is likely
actions: Refer to a mental health professional for grief-focused cognitive behavioural therapy or complicated grief treatment, which have the strongest evidence (Treatment of complicated grief, Section Effect sizes).
Treat comorbid depression with the depression pathway; antidepressants may help people engage in grief therapy but have no proven grief-specific effect (Pharmacotherapy review, Section Combination).

clinicalManagement.title: Act on suicide or psychosis
actions: Assess suicide risk, keep the person safe, and arrange urgent psychiatric assessment (NICE NG222 depression guideline, Recommendation 1.2.8 and 1.2.9).

medicationPlan.note: No medicine is indicated for normal grief. For prolonged grief disorder the best evidence is for grief-focused psychotherapy. Antidepressants are considered only for comorbid major depression, with open-label SSRI studies suggesting a possible additional benefit when combined with grief therapy and no proven grief-specific effect; benzodiazepines did not help and are not advised (Pharmacotherapy review, Section Benzodiazepines). Treat depression by the depression topic. SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so no medicine registration was checked.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Longing for or preoccupation with the deceased plus intense emotional pain, persisting more than 6 months after the loss, exceeding cultural, social or religious norms, with significant impairment (ICD-11 prolonged grief disorder review, Section Table 1).
At least 6 months since the death (ICD-11 prolonged grief disorder review, Section Table 1).
Prolonged Grief-13 score of 32 or more in Saudi students (Arabic-speaking cohort, Section Introduction); not a diagnostic cut-off.
Significant impairment beyond 6 months, or earlier if suicidal, psychotic or unable to function (ICD-11 prolonged grief disorder review, Section Table 1).

learningObjectives: Recognise normal grief and support it without medicalising.
Diagnose prolonged grief disorder only after 6 months and beyond cultural norms.
Refer for grief-focused therapy and avoid benzodiazepines.
keyPoints: Women, close family loss and low support raise risk.
Grief therapy, not drugs, is the main treatment.

patientEducation: Grief is a natural response; sadness, tears and poor sleep are expected and usually ease with time.
Lean on family, friends and your faith community.
Eat, sleep and keep daily routines as you are able.
Seek help if you cannot function after 6 months, or at any time if you have thoughts of ending your life.
Sleeping tablets and tranquillisers are not advised for grief.
lifestyleAndDiet: Keep regular meals and sleep times.
Take part in prayer and religious practice that comforts you.
mdtReferrals: Primary care physician; nurse; social worker; psychologist; psychiatrist; hospital chaplain or religious affairs staff; palliative care team when the death followed a terminal illness.
dischargeCriteria: Relevant contact numbers; named follow-up in primary care; written advice on warning signs and urgent help.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Contact at about 1 and 3 months for higher-risk people; structured review at 6 months for persistent impairment; urgent review for suicide risk at any time.
